# Inference {#sec-sys-inference}

Inference is where a trained model meets real traffic. This chapter
explains how serving got the shape it has: why modern systems batch the way
they do, why a cache dominates their memory, and what limits decoding speed
in principle. By the end a reader can explain why an inference service
behaves as it does under load, not only how to configure one.

## Problem

A forward pass is expensive and a request is small. Serving one request per
process leaves the accelerator idle most of the time. The constraints are
latency budget, concurrency, memory, and cost per request.

## Design

Continuous batching and a key-value cache: fold many in-flight requests
into one accelerator pass, and reuse the attention state that
autoregressive decoding would otherwise recompute every step.

## Evolution

From request-per-process serving, to static batching, to the continuous
batching and paged attention introduced by systems like Orca and vLLM.
Trace why each step was forced by the one before it.

## Trade-offs

Batching trades latency for throughput until the queue dominates.
Quantization trades precision for footprint. Each optimization must be
checked against the outputs it is supposed to preserve.

## In practice

Operational reality: latency percentiles, tokens per second, cost per
request, load shedding, timeouts, and graceful degradation. Minimal sketch
of a continuous-batching scheduler loop.

## Foundations

Why the behavior holds. Arithmetic intensity and the roofline model, why
batching moves a workload along it, the redundancy the KV cache removes,
and the conditions under which speculative decoding is provably faster.

$$
\text{intensity} = \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{bytes moved}}
$$
